In [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] [[mathematics]], specifically in [[Combinatorial design|combinatorial design theory]] and [[combinatorial matrix theory]], the '''Williamson conjecture''' is that Williamson matrices of order <math>n</math> exist for all positive [[integer]]s <math>n</math>.
Four [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] and [[circulant matrix|circulant]] [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>, <math>D</math> are called ''Williamson matrices'' if their entries are <math>\pm1</math> and they satisfy the relationship

:<math>A^2 + B^2 + C^2 + D^2 = 4n\, I</math>

where <math>I</math> is the [[identity matrix]] of order <math>n</math>.  [[John Williamson (mathematician)|John Williamson]] showed that if <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>, <math>D</math> are Williamson matrices then

:<math>\begin{bmatrix}
  A &  B &  C &  D \\
 -B &  A & -D &  C \\
 -C &  D &  A & -B \\
 -D & -C &  B &  A
\end{bmatrix}</math>

is an [[Hadamard matrix]] of order <math>4n</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Williamson
 |first=John
 |title=Hadamard's determinant theorem and the sum of four squares
 |journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]]
 |volume=11
 |issue=1
 |pages=65–81
 |year=1944
 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-44-01108-7
 |mr=0009590}}</ref>
It was once considered likely that Williamson matrices exist for all orders <math>n</math>
and that the structure of Williamson matrices could provide a route to proving the [[Hadamard conjecture]] that Hadamard matrices exist for all orders <math>4n</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Golomb
 |first1=Solomon W.
 |last2=Baumert
 |first2=Leonard D.
 |title=The Search for Hadamard Matrices
 |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 |volume=70
 |issue=1
 |pages=12–17
 |year=1963
 |doi=10.2307/2312777
 |jstor=2312777
 |mr=0146195}}</ref>
However, in 1993 the Williamson conjecture was shown to be false by Dragomir Ž. Ðoković through an exhaustive computer search, which demonstrated that Williamson matrices do not exist of order <math>n=35</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last = Ðoković
 |first = Dragomir Ž.
 |title = Williamson matrices of order <math>4n</math> for <math>n = 33, 35, 39</math>
 |journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 |volume = 115
 |issue = 1
 |pages = 267–271
 |year = 1993
 |doi = 10.1016/0012-365X(93)90495-F
 |mr=1217635
|doi-access = free
 }}</ref>  In 2008, the [[counterexample]]s 47, 53, and 59 were additionally discovered.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1 = Holzmann
 |first1 = W. H.
 |last2 = Kharaghani
 |first2 = H.
 |last3 = Tayfeh-Rezaie
 |first3 = B.
 |title = Williamson matrices up to order 59
 |journal = Designs, Codes and Cryptography
 |volume = 46
 |issue = 3
 |pages = 343–352
 |year = 2008
 |doi = 10.1007/s10623-007-9163-5
 |mr=2372843
}}</ref> 

Following the negative result of Ðoković, which ruled out the existence of Williamson matrices of order <math>n=35</math>, it was shown in 2019 that relaxing the symmetry and circulant requirements nevertheless permits a Hadamard matrix of this block form to exist for that order.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kline |first=Jeffery |title=Geometric search for Hadamard matrices |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |volume=778 |pages=33–46 |date=26 July 2019 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2019.01.025}}</ref> One such instance is given by the sequences
<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
a = --+--+--+++-+----+-+++--+--+-------
b = +---+---+-++-+--+-++-+---+---++++++
c = -++---+-+--+--++--+++++-+-+++++-+--
d = +----+++-+-+--++--+-+-+++----++---+
</syntaxhighlight>
with the associated matrices defined by
<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
A = circulant(a)
B = circulant(b)
C = fliplr(circulant(c))
D = circulant(d)
</syntaxhighlight>
